warmup.q: cass3 freezes in a long garbage-collection pause and sends nothing. With Cassandra 5.0's defaults, about how long until cass1 marks it DOWN?
options: About 1 second: gossip runs every second, so one missed round is enough
About 20 seconds: suspicion grows with the silence and passes the threshold after about 18 average gaps
Never by itself: only an operator can mark a node down
warmup.why: Cassandra's phi accrual detector compares the silence with the usual gap between heartbeats (about 1 second on a small cluster) and convicts when phi = 0.434 × silence / mean gap passes 8, after about 18.4 seconds; the Try-it in section 4 measured 20. One missed round is normal jitter. The 3 hours is how long hints are kept for a down node. And an operator is only needed to remove a node from the ring for good: marking it down is automatic and local to each node.

sections.h: A cluster of equal peers, each with its own map of the cluster
sections.html:
This lesson starts the track's case studies: each one takes a real system and shows the track's ideas working together. Cassandra uses three you have already met. Lessons 1 and 2 gave it hash partitioning on a token ring with 16 tokens per node. The Replication track's lesson on leaderless replication gave it quorums, hints and read repair. Lesson 3 gave it a routing rule: any node may coordinate any request. All three rest on something a cluster without a master has to build for itself. Every node must hold the map of the cluster and know who in it is alive. That map is this lesson's subject.

Send a write for A-1001 to cass2 and cass2 handles it. The Replication track called that node the coordinator: any node can take any request, and there is no master to ask. So before cass2 can do anything, it has to answer two questions on its own. Which nodes hold A-1001's copies? And which of them are alive right now?

The obvious design keeps the answers in one place. A master holds the map of the cluster, the other nodes ask it or receive updates from it, and it decides who is down. HBase works that way, and so does Kafka with its KRaft controller, a Raft group (the Consensus track builds Raft). It costs something Dynamo's designers wouldn't pay. While the master is down or being re-elected, nobody learns about changes, and every change in a cluster of hundreds of nodes passes through it. The Dynamo paper lists symmetry as a design principle: every node has the same job as its peers. Cassandra 5.0 follows it.

So every node keeps its own copy of the whole map. For each node in the cluster it holds one small record: the address and host ID, the datacenter and rack, the 16 tokens, the state (NORMAL, joining, leaving, shut down), how much data it holds, its Cassandra release and the version of its schema. Cassandra calls this record the node's endpoint state. The map is small. A 1,000-node cluster has 16,000 tokens, a few hundred kilobytes of memory. Each node also saves its view in two tables, system.local for itself and system.peers_v2 for everybody else, so it can start from them after a restart.

From the map, every node works out the rest by itself. Placement is pure arithmetic: the same map and the same rules give the same replicas on every node, so cass1 and cass3 agree on where A-1001 lives without asking each other. Liveness is different. Each node runs its own failure detector and decides for itself whether a peer is up.

Every node holds the same map of the cluster (tokens, datacenters, racks, states), gossip keeps the copies in step, and each node decides for itself who is alive. Section 2 turns the map into replicas. Section 3 shows how gossip spreads a change, and how SWIM does it differently. Section 4 shows how a node decides that a peer is down, and section 5 follows one write and one read through all three.

sections.h: From a key to its replicas: tokens, the allocator, racks and the snitch
sections.html:
Lesson 2 built the ring: Murmur3 hashes a partition key to a 64-bit token, every node owns 16 tokens, and a key's copies go to the nodes that own the next tokens clockwise. It left three questions open. Where does Cassandra put a new node's 16 tokens? What happens with racks? And how does a node know which rack another node is in?

Tokens first. Random positions aren't good enough with 16 tokens: in lesson 2's demo one of six nodes got 24.3% of the ring against a fair 16.7%. Cassandra 3.x added a token allocator, and 5.0.9's cassandra.yaml turns it on with allocate_tokens_for_local_replication_factor: 3. The allocator is greedy. It places the new node's tokens one at a time, and for each one keeps the candidate position that brings every node's replicated load closest to the average. Replicated load is all the data a node holds as any of the copies, which is why the allocator needs the replication factor. Run offline for six nodes, it leaves the most loaded node at 1.02 times the average. A node chooses its tokens once, on its first start, so num_tokens and the allocator setting must be right before a node ever starts.

Then copies. SimpleStrategy takes the first RF distinct nodes on the walk and ignores racks and datacenters. NetworkTopologyStrategy (NTS) gives each datacenter its own count, such as {'dc1': 3, 'dc2': 3}, and inside each datacenter it spreads copies over racks. Cassandra 5.0's rule, from NetworkTopologyStrategy.java: walk the ring once; take a node whose rack holds no copy yet; skip a node whose rack already has one, unless the datacenter has fewer racks than copies, in which case the first (RF minus racks) repeats are taken. The figure walks one key. A rack is whatever fails together: one power feed and one top-of-rack switch in a data hall, or one availability zone in a cloud region. With three racks and RF 3, losing a whole rack still leaves two copies of every row, so QUORUM keeps working.

Racks have a trap. One copy per rack means a rack with fewer nodes gives each of its nodes a bigger share. With racks of 2, 2 and 1 nodes and RF 3, the lone node holds a copy of every row; the lab proves it. Keep racks the same size and grow them together.

Who knows the racks? Each node's snitch. GossipingPropertyFileSnitch, which the lab cluster uses and the docs recommend for production, reads the node's own datacenter and rack from cassandra-rackdc.properties and announces them in gossip, so DC and RACK are part of every node's map. The snitch also ranks replicas by closeness for reads. The dynamic snitch re-ranks them by measured latency every 100 ms; the lab cluster switches it off so a read stays on the local copy. Choose the snitch, datacenters and racks before the first write. cassandra.yaml warns that switching to an incompatible snitch once data is in the cluster loses data, because the replica sets would change under the data.

sections.h: Gossip: every second, three messages with one random peer
sections.html:
Every second, every Cassandra node picks another node at random and the two compare notes. That is the whole protocol. To see why, start from what has to happen when the map changes. A node joins and owns 16 new tokens. A node's load grows. Someone runs CREATE TABLE and every node gets a new schema. Every node has to hear each change, and every node has to keep hearing that every other node is still alive.

Version 1: whoever changes tells everyone, and every node sends a heartbeat to every other node once a second. That's N × (N − 1) messages a second just to say "still here": 870 for 30 nodes, about a million for 1,000. And a node that misses a message, because it was restarting or a link dropped it, never hears that news again.

Version 2: once a second, each node tells one random peer what it knows, and that peer passes it on in its own rounds. News spreads like an epidemic: one node knows, then two, then about four. The number that knows roughly doubles every round, so it reaches all N nodes in about log2 N rounds. The demo in the Try-it measures it: a median of 2 rounds for 6 nodes and 8 for 6,000, while a round costs 3 × N messages instead of N². Nothing is lost for good either: a node that missed the news hears it at its next exchange with anyone who has it.

Version 3 fixes the size of each message. "What I know" is the whole map, and sending it every second is wasteful when almost nothing changed. So every piece of state carries a version. Each node has one counter, and every heartbeat and every change to its own state takes the next number. With versions, two nodes start by swapping digests, three numbers per node: which node, which generation, highest version. That's GossipDigestSyn. The receiver compares each digest with its own copy and replies with GossipDigestAck: the states it has that are newer, plus requests for the ones that are newer at the sender. The sender applies them and answers the requests with GossipDigestAck2. Three messages, and only new state travels. The stepper runs it on six nodes.

The generation handles restarts. A restarted JVM starts its counter from zero, so its versions are smaller than what the cluster remembers. The generation is the node's start time in seconds since 1970, and a higher generation wins before versions are compared at all. In the Try-it, cass3 came back with generation 1794104511 and heartbeat 32, and every node replaced the old state, whose heartbeat had been set to 2147483647 when it shut down.

Seeds are contact points. A new node knows nobody, so cassandra.yaml lists a few seeds, and the node asks one of them for the whole map before it joins. After that a seed is an ordinary node that the others also gossip with now and then, which stops the cluster from splitting into groups that never hear each other. Seeds aren't masters. One rule matters: a seed never bootstraps, as cass1 logged at startup ("This node will not auto bootstrap because it is configured to be a seed node"), so a new node must not be in its own seed list.

Cassandra's way isn't the only way to gossip membership. SWIM (Das, Gupta and Motivala, 2002), which HashiCorp's memberlist library runs inside Consul, Nomad and Serf, splits the job in two. To detect failures, each member pings one random member per protocol period, and if no ack comes back it asks k other members to ping that member for it. To spread news it sends nothing extra: membership changes ride on the pings and acks that go out anyway. The paper measured about 2 messages per member per period, one ping and one ack, whatever the group size. A failure is first noticed after e / (e − 1), about 1.6, periods on average, and the news reaches everyone in a few periods, growing with log N. Cassandra ships versioned state and leaves detection to each receiver. SWIM probes on purpose and gossips only what changed.

sections.h: Failure detection: phi turns silence into a level of suspicion
sections.html:
In the Try-it below, cass1 marks a frozen cass3 DOWN 20 seconds after it froze. Nobody told cass1; it decided from silence alone. Silence is the only evidence a node has: a frozen JVM, a dead machine and a cut cable look the same from the other side, as newer heartbeats that stop arriving through gossip. (The Faults, time and truth track treats timeouts in general.)

Version 1 is a fixed timeout: no newer heartbeat for 5 seconds means down. It breaks because heartbeats don't arrive on a schedule. A heartbeat reaches cass1 only when some exchange carries it, so the gaps vary, and they grow across an ocean or when a node is busy. A timeout tight enough for a LAN marks healthy nodes down and up again on a WAN; one loose enough for the WAN is slow on the LAN.

Version 2 learns what normal looks like and measures silence against it. That is the phi accrual failure detector of Hayashibara and colleagues (2004), and Cassandra runs a variant of it. For every peer, a node keeps the last 1,000 inter-arrival times, the gaps between newer heartbeats. Cassandra assumes the gaps follow an exponential distribution, so the chance that a healthy peer whose mean gap is m stays quiet for t seconds is e^(−t/m). Phi is minus the base-10 logarithm of that chance: phi = t / (m × ln 10), about 0.43 × t/m. Phi 1 means a healthy node is this quiet one time in 10, phi 8 one time in 100 million. The node convicts the peer when phi passes phi_convict_threshold. In 5.0.9's cassandra.yaml that line is commented out at its default of 8, with the advice that most users never need to change it. Akka's cluster uses the same threshold of 8 with a normal distribution instead, and its docs suggest 12 on EC2, where gaps vary more.

Now the numbers. A heartbeat version moves once a second at its source, so on the lab cluster m is about 1 second and phi crosses 8 after 8 × 2.303 × 1 s = 18.4 seconds of silence. The check runs once a second, which is how cass1 got to about 20. Two guards keep the detector sane. Gaps longer than 2 seconds are never recorded, so one outage doesn't teach it patience. And a node that was itself frozen for more than 5 seconds marks nobody down: when cass3 woke up, it logged Not marking nodes down due to local pause of 35664433642ns > 5000000000ns, because from its point of view everybody had been silent for 35 seconds.

That second guard points at the problem SWIM's designers kept working on. In SWIM a member that misses its probes is first suspected, not declared dead, and the suspicion travels in gossip. The suspected member hears it and refutes it with a higher incarnation number, a counter only it may raise. Lifeguard (Dadgar, Phillips and Currey at HashiCorp, 2017) found that most remaining false alarms came from the detecting member being slow itself, a busy or paused process missing acks that had arrived. So each member keeps a local health score from its own failed probes and refutations, and stretches its timeouts while that score is bad. A suspicion's timeout also starts long and shrinks as independent members confirm it. In their tests false positives fell more than 50 times with no slower detection. Cassandra's local-pause guard is a blunt version of the same idea.

Down is a local decision, and down isn't gone. UP and DOWN aren't propagated with gossip: in an earlier freeze on the same cluster, cass2 convicted cass3 half a second before cass1 did. A clean shutdown is announced in gossip, so peers mark the node down within a second without waiting for phi. And the node keeps its tokens, because Cassandra never removes a node from the ring without an operator's instruction. While a coordinator sees cass3 as down, it counts it as missing for consistency levels, sends it no reads, and keeps hints for its writes for up to max_hint_window, 3 hours. The stepper follows phi through a freeze.

sections.h: One write and one read through a coordinator
sections.html:
Follow one write of A-2002's balance at QUORUM, sent to cass2, through everything above. The Try-it traces it.

  1. cass2 hashes the partition key: Murmur3 turns 'A-2002' into the token 1517767796525818520.
  2. It walks its own copy of the ring with NetworkTopologyStrategy. The first token at or after the key is cass3's, the next cass1's, then cass3's again (skipped) and then cass2's. The replicas are cass3, cass1 and cass2, in the order nodetool getendpoints printed.
  3. It asks its failure detector which replicas are up and compares with the consistency level. QUORUM of three needs two. All three are up, so it goes ahead. With two down it would answer Unavailable and send nothing.
  4. It sends the mutation to every live replica, whatever the consistency level, and writes its own copy the way the Data models track's wide-column lesson described: commit log, then memtable. A replica it believes down gets a hint instead.
  5. It answers the client as soon as two replicas have acknowledged. In the trace, cass2's own write and cass3's reply made two, and the request completed 0.45 seconds before cass1's reply arrived; cass1 applied the write anyway. If fewer than two replies come back within write_request_timeout, 2 seconds here, the client gets WriteTimeout, and the coordinator keeps hints for the replicas that stayed silent.

A read at QUORUM repeats steps 1 to 3 and then asks fewer nodes. The snitch sorts the live replicas by closeness: the coordinator itself first if it's a replica, then by the dynamic snitch's latency scores when that's on. The coordinator asks the closest for the data and the next one for a digest, a hash of its answer. Equal digests end the read; different ones start the read repair from the Replication track. In the trace, cass2 read its own copy, took a digest from cass3, and never asked cass1.

Clients usually save one hop, the shard-aware client of lesson 3. The Java driver reads the same map from system.peers_v2, gets topology changes pushed by the node it's connected to, and computes a prepared statement's token itself, so it sends each request straight to a replica, which coordinates locally. The 4.x driver's default load-balancing policy does this token-aware routing whenever the statement carries its routing key. The driver judges which nodes are up from its own connections; it doesn't run phi.

refs.title: Apache Cassandra 5.0: Dynamo (tunable consistency, picking consistency levels)

analogy: Picture an office with no manager. Every clerk keeps a copy of the staff directory: each colleague's desk, floor and current status, with a last-updated stamp on every entry. Once a minute each clerk phones one colleague at random, and the two read out their stamps. Whoever has an older entry copies the newer one. A change made on one desk reaches the whole office in a handful of minutes, and nobody had to be in charge. Each clerk also notices, for each colleague, how often they usually hear news from them, and gets suspicious when the silence runs much longer than usual. The analogy breaks on the phone itself: a real clerk who gets no answer knows the call failed, while a Cassandra node only ever sees the absence of newer heartbeats, and it can't tell a dead colleague from a slow line.
world: Your Kafka cluster is the opposite design: a KRaft controller quorum holds the metadata and tells brokers what changed. Cassandra has no such component, so there is nothing to fail over, and also nobody who knows the truth for certain. Your Quarkus services see this through the Java driver. It reads system.peers_v2 at startup, gets topology events pushed over its control connection, and sends prepared statements straight to a replica. When a node freezes in a long GC pause, its peers keep counting it as up for about 20 seconds, so requests routed to it, or waiting on it as a replica, time out in that window. Give the driver a request timeout your payment API can live with, use LOCAL_QUORUM so one slow replica doesn't block a write, and use speculative executions only on reads and on writes that are safe to retry, such as an idempotent upsert keyed by the payment id.
mistake: The most common mistake is treating seeds as special servers. Teams list every node as a seed "to be safe", or start a new node with its own address in its seed list because the template said so. A seed never bootstraps, so the new node joins the ring at once, claims its 16 token ranges, and streams nothing: reads at ONE that land on it return no rows, and QUORUM reads lean on read repair until someone runs a full repair. The opposite mistake, one seed in total, means a new node can't join while that machine is down. The fix: two or three seeds per datacenter, stable long-lived nodes, the same list on every node, and never a node that is joining for the first time. Seeds matter only when a node starts and as preferred gossip partners; nothing else depends on them.

compare.title: Who keeps the map: a leader, or every node

a.label: A leader keeps it (Kafka's KRaft controller, a Raft group)
a.title: A leader keeps it (Kafka's KRaft controller, a Raft group)
a.html:
one elected leader holds the cluster metadata
  changes:   a write to the leader's log, replicated to a quorum
  followers: learn changes from the leader, in one order
  liveness:  the leader decides who is in, from heartbeats

every node    -> sees the same order of changes

b.html:
every node holds the whole map, versioned per node
  changes:   a node bumps its own state's version
  spreading: one random peer a second, Syn / Ack / Ack2
  liveness:  each node runs its own phi detector

any node dies -> nothing to elect; the others carry on
every node    -> converges in about log N rounds, no global order

compare.note: A leader gives one order of changes and one answer to "is this node in the cluster?", and pays with an election whenever the leader fails. Gossip has no single point to fail, and costs a little delay and the chance that two nodes briefly disagree: cass1 and cass2 marked cass3 down half a second apart. Cassandra 6.0 (in alpha) moves membership, tokens and schema into a Cluster Metadata Service that orders every change in one log, for exactly that reason, and keeps gossip for heartbeats and load.

worked.title: Place A-2002 and follow its write, by hand

steps.say: Hash the partition key. The lab's TokenRing.murmur3 is Cassandra's Murmur3Partitioner, and it gives the number token(account_id) prints.
steps.code: TokenRing.murmur3("A-2002") // 1517767796525818520, on every machine

steps.say: Find the first token at or after the key in nodetool ring, then walk on, keeping distinct nodes until there are three. Here every node is in rack1, so NetworkTopologyStrategy skips only repeats of a node.
steps.code:
1457039303564410890  cass2   the range (1457..., 1888...] holds the key
1888050784495078973  cass3   first token at or after the key: copy 1
2154768217990839511  cass1   copy 2
2554981533416019809  cass3   already a replica: skip
2807241130139088773  cass2   copy 3

steps.say: Check liveness and the consistency level before sending anything. This is the step that turns into Unavailable when too many replicas are down.
steps.code:
replicas          cass3, cass1, cass2
alive (phi < 8)   all three
QUORUM of RF 3    2 needed, 3 alive  -> send

with cass1 and cass3 down: 1 alive -> Unavailable, nothing sent

steps.say: Send the mutation to all live replicas and count acknowledgements. The coordinator is a replica here, so its own write counts as one.
steps.code:
t = 0 ms     cass2 writes locally (commit log, memtable)   ack 1
t = 64 ms    cass3 acknowledges                            ack 2 -> reply to the client
t = 701 ms   cass1 acknowledges                            applied, nobody waits

steps.say: The read repeats placement and liveness, then asks only as many replicas as the level needs: the data from the closest, a digest from the next.
steps.code:
sorted by the snitch   cass2 (itself), cass3, cass1
data                   cass2's own copy: balance_minor 4200
digest                 cass3's hash of its answer
equal                  -> answer the client; cass1 is never asked
different              -> fetch full data, keep the newest, read repair

lab.title: Build gossip, a phi accrual detector and rack-aware placement
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. No Docker needed. 21 of 22 fail with NotImplementedError; the one that checks the given murmur3 against the tokens Cassandra printed in lesson 2 already passes.

In PhiAccrual.kt, write heartbeat (record the gap, but never one longer than maxIntervalMillis, and keep at most windowSize) and phi (one line). The six PhiAccrualTest tests pass, including the one that puts conviction at 18.4 seconds.

In Placement.kt, write networkTopology: walk the ring once with the given walk, keep books per datacenter (wanted copies, rack repeats allowed, racks used) and follow the rule in the KDoc. The last test checks you against nodetool getendpoints output captured from the lab cluster.
In Gossip.kt, write examine (the five cases in its KDoc) and apply (generation first, then versions). GossipCluster, which runs rounds, Syn, Ack and Ack2 between your nodes, is given. All 22 pass.
Experiment: in apply, compare versions only and ignore the generation. Run the tests again: the restart tests fail, because a restarted node's small versions lose to its old life. Put it back.
hints: ArrayDeque has addLast and removeFirst. The first heartbeat has no previous one, so it records initialIntervalMillis; the gap check only applies after that.
phi is PHI_FACTOR * (nowMillis - last) / meanMillis. Return 0.0 while lastHeartbeatMillis is null.
For the books, endpoints.groupBy { it.dc } gives each datacenter's nodes; the rack count is nodes.map { it.rack }.toSet().size. HashSet.add returns false when the rack was already there.

In examine, a when with the cases in order reads well: unknown or higher generation there, lower generation there, higher version there, lower version there. local.newerThan(v)!! is safe because you only call it when ours is newer.

In apply, skip ep == name, then replace the whole state when remote.generation > local.generation. With equal generations, merge state by state, keeping the higher version, and report the endpoint when remote.heartbeat > local.heartbeat.

drill.title: The Syn receiver and phi, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the body of examine(syn: List<Digest>): Ack for a gossip node whose map is endpoints: Map<String, EndpointState>. Then write the phi formula Cassandra uses and work out when a peer with a mean gap of 1 second is convicted.

answer.html: fun examine(syn: List<Digest>): Ack { val requests = mutableListOf<Digest>() val states = sortedMapOf<String, EndpointState>() for (d in syn) { val local = endpoints[d.endpoint] when { // never heard of it, or it restarted: ask for everything local == null || d.generation > local.generation -> requests += Digest(d.endpoint, d.generation, 0) // the sender still has the old life of this node: send everything d.generation < local.generation -> states[d.endpoint] = local.newerThan(0)!! // same life: compare one version number d.maxVersion > local.maxVersion -> requests += Digest(d.endpoint, d.generation, local.maxVersion) d.maxVersion < local.maxVersion -> states[d.endpoint] = local.newerThan(d.maxVersion)!! } } return Ack(requests, states) } // phi = (silence / mean gap) / ln 10, about 0.434 * t / m // convicted when phi > 8: t > 8 * ln 10 * m = 18.4 s for m = 1 s

recap: Every Cassandra node keeps the whole map of the cluster (tokens, datacenter, rack, state, load, schema) and works out replicas by itself; there is no master.

Tokens: 16 per node, placed by the replication-aware allocator (allocate_tokens_for_local_replication_factor: 3) to within about 2% of even. NetworkTopologyStrategy then walks the ring per datacenter and spreads copies over racks; keep racks equal in size.

Gossip: every second each node exchanges Syn, Ack and Ack2 with one random peer. Versions say what's new, the generation (start time) wins across restarts, and news reaches N nodes in about log N rounds. Seeds only introduce starting nodes, and a seed never bootstraps.
Phi accrual: phi = 0.434 × silence / mean gap; past 8 (about 18 to 20 seconds on the lab cluster) a node marks a peer down, locally. Down means hints and no reads, not removal.

SWIM probes one random member per period, asks k others when a ping goes unanswered, and piggybacks changes on its pings: about 2 messages per member per period at any size. Suspicion with incarnation numbers, and Lifeguard's local health, cut false alarms (more than 50 times in Lifeguard's tests).
A coordinator hashes the key, walks its ring, checks live replicas against the consistency level, sends the write to all live replicas and answers after enough acknowledgements.

explain.prompt: A new teammate asks: "If Cassandra has no master, how does cass2 know where A-1001 lives and whether cass3 is alive, and how does it learn that a fourth node just joined?" Answer in a few sentences.
explain.answer: Every node keeps its own copy of the whole cluster map: for each node its tokens, datacenter, rack, state, load and schema version. Placement is computed from that map: cass2 hashes A-1001 with Murmur3, walks the token ring clockwise and takes three distinct nodes, spreading them over racks with NetworkTopologyStrategy, and every node gets the same answer because the map and the rules are the same. Liveness is local: cass2's phi accrual detector watches how often newer heartbeats of cass3 arrive and marks it down when the silence is about 18 times the usual gap. The map stays in step through gossip. Every second each node exchanges digests with one random peer (Syn, Ack, Ack2), and only states with newer versions travel. When cass4 joins, it bumps its own STATUS and TOKENS; within a few rounds every node has heard it, because the number of nodes that know roughly doubles each round. A restart is recognised by a larger generation, the node's start time.

deeper.html:
Gossip carries more than this lesson used. nodetool gossipinfo on a 5.0 node also shows RPC_READY (the node accepts CQL), NET_VERSION, SSTABLE_VERSIONS and, for the local node only, a few legacy states such as INTERNAL_IP and the old STATUS next to STATUS_WITH_PORT. Since 4.0 every address is gossiped with its port, so several nodes can share one IP address.

A starting node runs a shadow round before it gossips normally: it sends an empty Syn to its seeds and they answer with their whole map, so the node can check, for instance, that no live node already owns its address. That is the main thing seeds are for.

The failure detector's local-pause guard exists because a node coming out of a long GC pause sees every peer silent for, say, 35 seconds. Without the guard it would convict the whole cluster and flip everyone back to UP a second later. The cap on recorded gaps (cassandra.fd_max_interval_ms, 2 seconds by default, which the startup log mentions as Overriding cassandra.fd_max_interval_ms) keeps an outage from inflating the mean. The original phi accrual paper assumed normally distributed gaps; Cassandra's exponential assumption makes phi a straight line in the silence, which is what failuredetector showed.

Cassandra 6.0, in alpha, takes membership, tokens and schema away from gossip with Transactional Cluster Metadata (CEP-21): a Cluster Metadata Service on a few nodes orders every change to the ring in one log, so two nodes can't hold different rings, and a bootstrap or decommission becomes a sequence of logged steps. Gossip stays for heartbeats and load. The trade is the one in the compare box: one order of changes, in exchange for a small group of nodes that has to be up for the ring to change.

Schema travels by gossip too. Each node gossips SCHEMA, a UUID of its table definitions; a node that sees a different one pulls the schema from that peer, and nodetool describecluster lists every version in the cluster (one, when they agree).

The move away from gossip-held metadata is wider than Cassandra. ScyllaDB switched topology changes to Raft in its 6.0 release, and Kafka 4.0 removed ZooKeeper for its own Raft quorum. Gossip keeps the job it does well, spreading heartbeats and load cheaply, while ownership of ranges goes to a log that every node reads in the same order.

One more way to read this lesson's outputs: nodetool status is a view of gossip (state and load from the map) plus the local failure detector (the U or D), while nodetool ring and describering are pure arithmetic over the tokens in the map.
